title: The Song We Keep
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 39 of 40
content:
Greg had written the last line of the song three times.

On the first scrap of paper, it promised a forever neither of us had asked for.

On the second, it sounded like somebody leaving before they could be left.

On the third, the line stopped halfway through.

He put all three beside his guitar and stared at them.

"I think I've invented a new kind of writer's block," he announced.

"What's it called?"

"Having feelings and being annoying about them."

I laughed, then saw he wasn't quite joking.

We were in the garage, surrounded by cables, a small recording device, and a box of things Greg had been meaning to sort for months. The air smelled of warm dust and sea salt. One wall held posters from shows I'd never attended; another held a shelf with spare strings and the battered notebook where he kept chord progressions.

The song had begun beside Starwake Pier, where water made a low note beneath the wooden boards. Greg had copied part of that rhythm into the melody, leaving a long pause after the fifth note. He liked the pause when he played alone. Every time he tried to finish the lyrics, he filled it with a promise too large to trust.

"Play the beginning again?" I asked.

He picked up the guitar.

The opening was gentle and slightly crooked. I knew the melody well enough to hum along, though I still missed the turn in the third phrase.

Greg stopped.

"That's the wrong harmony."

"Sorry."

"No, wait. Do it again."

I hummed.

He listened, then picked out a new chord beneath it.

"Oh," he said.

"Good oh?"

"Interesting oh. That's the kind that gets you in trouble."

He played it again. The new chord made the next note sound uncertain, almost as though the tune had reached a doorway and didn't know whether to step through.

"Keep that," I said.

Greg set down the guitar.

"You're not just saying that to be nice?"

"No. I actually like the way it doesn't resolve."

He stared at the unfinished line.

"That's the problem."

I waited.

"If I finish it," he said, "people might think I'm promising something about us. Like the song's a contract."

"Do you think that?"

"Sometimes I worry I'll start believing it."

He looked embarrassed, and I knew how much it had cost him to admit it. Greg was generous with laughter. Fear was harder. He tended to pack it inside a joke and hope the music would do the rest.

I sat on the overturned crate beside him.

"We can write a song without making it a binding agreement."

"Sure. But then I get scared that if it's not a big promise, it doesn't mean enough."

I thought about the green notebook in my bag, the one with my living agreements and the things I was learning to ask for.

"Can I tell you something without turning it into a verse?"

He smiled.

"Please."

"I love you. I am ethically non-monogamous and prefer polyamory, and we've already talked about that honestly. I don't want the song to erase those choices. I don't want it to make you a consolation prize, either."

Greg looked down at his hands.

"That's the part I'm bad at."

"Which part?"

"Believing I matter without being the only one."

I felt my chest tighten.

"I can't prove you matter by making somebody else disappear."

"I know."

"But I can tell you why you're here with me. Because I like your terrible jokes. Because you listen when I say a plan isn't working. Because you remember what I drink when I get distracted. Because you can be scared and still choose to tell me."

He breathed out slowly.

"That's a pretty good list."

"There's also the van."

"Ah. The real reason."

"The seats are surprisingly comfortable."

He laughed, and it eased something in the room.

He reached for my hand.

"Can I ask you for a date next week?"

"Yes. I have an afternoon free after Moonroot."

"Just us?"

"Just us. If the archive runs late, I'll send word instead of leaving you guessing."

"Deal."

We sat for a while, listening to the little recording device hum.

Then I picked up the third page.

"What if the last line isn't about forever? What if it's about something we keep doing, one time at a time?"

Greg looked at me.

"Like what?"

"Listening."

He considered.

"Too much like a public service announcement."

"Coming back?"

"Too much like a ferry schedule."

I grinned.

"You're impossible."

"Artistically sensitive."

"Same thing."

He played the melody again. This time he left the space open, and I hummed my wrong harmony over the next chord. It didn't resolve neatly. It sounded like two people who had heard each other and still had different ways of reaching the same place.

Greg's eyes lit up.

"That's it."

"What?"

"We don't need another line."

"Seriously?"

"The space is the line."

I stared.

"Greg."

"What?"

"That's either brilliant or you've avoided writing words so successfully you've declared silence a lyric."

He grinned.

"Both can be true."

We tested the song on the little recording device. The first take had a creaking chair in the middle of the pause. The second caught the sound of a truck backing up outside. On the third, Greg missed a chord because I'd made him laugh.

We kept the third.

It sounded like us.

Later we took the guitar down to the pier. The boards were dry, the safety notices were posted, and the wind carried the smell of the ocean through the railings. Greg checked the stage schedule with the volunteer steward before setting up. We weren't there to take over a public performance space; we wanted five minutes to hear how the new chord sounded outdoors.

A young busker was already playing near the bench.

"Mind if we wait?" Greg asked.

The musician shook their head.

"Not at all. I've got ten minutes left."

We listened until their set finished, then helped move the stand to storage. Greg played our song for the open air.

The last phrase hung between the sea and the wooden railing.

No triumphant resolution.

No tragic ending.

A breath.

I leaned against the post.

"What do you think?" I asked.

Greg looked at the page, then at me.

"I think I'm done trying to make this song answer questions it wasn't asked."

I smiled.

"That's a good place to stop."

He set the guitar in its case.

"May I kiss you?"

"Yes."

He kissed me warmly, one hand against my cheek, and pulled back with a laugh when a gust of wind blew his hair into my face.

"Very romantic."

"I was aiming for majestic."

"You hit ridiculous."

"Close enough."

On the way home, Greg stopped at the empty rehearsal hall to return a borrowed microphone stand.

The caretaker was stacking chairs. She glanced at the notebook under Greg's arm.

“Finished your big song?”

“Mostly,” Greg said. “I left a space at the end.”

“Can't sell a space on a record.”

“Good thing I'm not selling one tonight.”

The caretaker shrugged and carried on. Greg looked almost embarrassed by how much the exchange had mattered.

“Old me would've rewritten the whole thing before she could ask again,” he admitted.

I shifted the guitar case against my hip. “Old you might've had a completely different song to write.”

“Yeah. He was kind of a mess.”

“He was also a musician.”

Greg looked at me, then back at the door. “I think I keep trying to apologize for him and make sure he gets a standing ovation. Both at once. Not super efficient.”

“No. But it's an impressive workload.”

He laughed. We walked the rest of the way slowly. The boardwalk smelled of fried dough and salt; someone had left a paper cup beneath the bench. Greg stopped to pick it up and put it in the bin without making it a gesture worth announcing.

At the van, he asked whether I wanted to hear the last verse again. I did. He played it quietly, and the unfinished space arrived where it belonged. We listened to the sea move beneath the melody.

“I used to think every song needed to explain why somebody stayed,” he said.

“Does this one?”

He shook his head. “I think it just needs to remember we both got to choose.”

I leaned close and kissed the corner of his mouth before he could make a joke out of the sentence. He smiled, the guitar resting against his knee, and I could feel the laughter he was holding back.

It wasn't an answer to every question. It was a song with room for the next thing that happened.


At home, we put the third page in the song notebook. We kept the earlier drafts, too, because they were part of how we'd reached this version. Greg wrote a small note beside the empty final line:

*Leave room for the next day.*

That evening we ate dinner from paper cartons and watched the light move across the garage floor. The rest of our time stayed private; no lyric, no performance, no audience.

In the morning, Greg played the unfinished song once more.

He stopped at the open space.

This time he smiled before the next chord.

It was finished enough to keep living.
